bugs: Bad filter values on the GET catalogue (IndexProductRequest) trigger a validation redirect back. The previous URL is stored even on the redirect response, so two bad filter URLs in a row redirect to each other. A probe using followingRedirects ran out of memory in a redirect loop. A stale category slug in a shared link can do the same through the Referer header. impl-2 has the same issue.
antipatterns: resources/views/products/index.blade.php:20 builds the sort options with collect($sorts)->mapWithKeys(...) inside the view. This mapping belongs in the controller or the enum.
resources/views/products/show.blade.php:10 calls trans_choice with two identical plural forms. It adds nothing.
app/Http/Requests/IndexProductRequest.php: invalid GET filters are rejected with a redirect when they could just be ignored or fall back to defaults (see the redirect loop above).
resources/views/pagination/catalogue.blade.php: a full custom pagination view is extra code where a built-in one with a few CSS rules would do. Acceptable because there is no asset build.
strengths: The form.input, form.select, form.textarea, form.checkbox and form.error components use @props and $attributes->class()->merge(). The same form.select component is reused for the public category and sort filters.
x-flash uses the @session directive. Messages are wrapped in __() throughout.
Uses Gate::define('admin') with can:admin middleware and @can in the layout. It is simple and does the job.

Model uses #[Scope] attribute scopes (active, search, inCategory, sortedBy), a formatted_price Attribute accessor, and a related() method with whereBelongsTo and whereKeyNot. Related products are eager-loaded with category, and lazy loading is avoided under shouldBeStrict.
The LIKE search escapes wildcards with '!', which is portable across SQLite, MySQL and Postgres. Ordering has a stable id tie-break.
withQueryString() keeps filters across pages. Slug is generated from the name in prepareForValidation. Uniqueness uses Rule::unique()->ignore() with the route model.
Pest tests use datasets for sorts, validation, invalid filters and access control. They also cover old input, inline errors, flash messages and the no-compiled-assets check.

bugs: app/Models/Product.php:58-59 uses whereRaw("... like ? escape '\\'"), which produces the SQL escape '\'. MySQL's default sql_mode treats the backslash inside a string literal as an escape character, so the literal is unterminated and every search fails with a syntax error. It works on SQLite only.
Bad filter values on the GET catalogue trigger a validation redirect back that can loop between invalid URLs, confirmed with a probe. impl-1 has the same issue.
antipatterns: app/Policies/ProductPolicy.php: create, update and delete are declared but never called. Only viewAny is used, as route-group middleware. A gate or a single ability would be enough.

resources/views/products/index.blade.php:9-25 writes the category and sort selects by hand instead of reusing the form.select component. Lines 29-31 dump all errors in one list instead of showing them next to each filter field.
resources/views/components/layouts/app.blade.php:59-61 uses @if (session('status')) {{ session('status') }} instead of the @session directive.
app/Enums/ProductSort.php:22-31 puts query-building logic (apply(Builder)) in the enum, so it is coupled to Eloquent. A model scope would be the more usual place.
app/Models/Product.php:40 makes formattedPrice() a plain method instead of an Attribute accessor. That is a small idiom miss.
app/Providers/AppServiceProvider.php:25 uses Paginator::useBootstrapFour() without Bootstrap, so it depends on hand-written CSS that mimics Bootstrap's class names.
resources/views/admin/products/index.blade.php:32 wraps links() in @if ($products->hasPages()), which is redundant because the paginator view already checks this.
strengths: A shared x-form.field wrapper component with a slot holds the label and @error, and the input, select and textarea components compose it.
Uses #[Scope] attribute scopes, including a relatedTo scope with whereBelongsTo and whereKeyNot. withQueryString() is used, and safe()->only() supplies the filter values.
The migration uses restrictOnDelete and composite indexes on (is_active, created_at) and (is_active, price).

The tests are strong. They use describe blocks and followingRedirects() to check inline errors and old input in the rendered HTML, and assert that the filter values stay selected and that empty filters are ignored. Pagination links are checked for the exact query string.

v.rationale:
Both implementations are close in structure: the same Form Requests, #[Scope] model scopes, enum-based sort, resource controller with to_route()->with(), shared product-form component, and inline-CSS layout. Both test suites pass (45 tests for impl-1, 44 for impl-2). My probes found the same behaviour in both: an unchecked checkbox stays unchecked after a failed submit, LIKE wildcards are escaped correctly on SQLite, and invalid GET filters can redirect in a loop.

impl-1 ranks first because:
- Its Blade use is more idiomatic. The form.select component is reused for the public filters, errors use a dedicated form.error component, flash messages use @session, and strings go through __().
- Its authorization is simpler: one Gate with can:admin. impl-2 has a policy where three of the four methods are never used.
- Its search escaping is portable across databases. impl-2's escape '\' would break every search on MySQL.

impl-2's tests are a little more thorough (rendered old input via followingRedirects, selected filter values, empty filters). That does not outweigh its latent MySQL bug, the error list that isn't shown next to each filter field, and the extra policy code.

bugs: Searching for "0" is ignored: Product::search uses `$query->when($term, ...)` and "0" is falsy, so /products?q=0 returns every product (confirmed with a probe). app/Models/Product.php:73. The same falsy-`when` pattern is in inCategory at app/Models/Product.php:85.

If someone opens /products?sort=bogus directly, the redirect sends them to the welcome page, which never renders $errors. They see neither the error nor the catalogue (routes/web.php:7, IndexProductRequest).
antipatterns: Logic in the view: `collect($sorts)->mapWithKeys(fn ($sort) => [$sort->value => $sort->label()])` builds the sort options inside the Blade template (resources/views/products/index.blade.php:20). This belongs in the controller or the enum.
Product::related() runs a query from a model instance method and uses a RELATED_LIMIT constant (app/Models/Product.php:23,52). That is more ceremony than a relatedTo scope.
A custom pagination view (resources/views/pagination/catalogue.blade.php) plus Paginator::defaultView. This works but adds code where a built-in simple view would do.

Every string is wrapped in __(), including trans_choice('{1} :count in stock|[2,*] :count in stock'), where both branches produce the same text (resources/views/products/show.blade.php:10). This is pointless ceremony.
cascadeOnDelete on category_id silently deletes products when a category is deleted (database/migrations/2026_01_01_000001_create_products_table.php:13).
The test helper builds route params with a convoluted inline ternary (tests/Feature/Admin/ProductManagementTest.php:27).
strengths: Uses modern Blade throughout: @session in the flash component, @props/$attributes->class()->merge() on form components, @selected/@checked, @error extracted into an <x-form.error> component.
One shared product-form component with a configurable submit label. Uses old() with the model value as fallback, and a hidden checkbox input so an unchecked box saves as inactive.
Thin controllers. Form requests use prepareForValidation to generate the slug, Rule::enum and Rule::unique()->ignore. Typed accessors on IndexProductRequest.
Modern Eloquent: #[Scope] attributes, #[Fillable], Attribute::get accessor, whereBelongsTo, whereRelation, LIKE wildcard escaping, deterministic tie-break ordering, eager loading of category.
Inline CSS, so pages render without compiled assets, and there is a test asserting that. The filter form reuses the shared select component.

bugs: An invalid filter query (for example ?sort=bogus) triggers a redirect-back from the GET form request instead of falling back to defaults. It recovers via / → /products, which shows the errors, but this UX is harsher than it needs to be (app/Http/Requests/IndexProductRequest.php).
antipatterns: The ProductSort enum has an apply(Builder) method, which puts query building inside an enum (app/Enums/ProductSort.php:22). A match inside the sortedBy scope would keep query logic on the model.

ProductPolicy has four identical is_admin methods, and the route middleware only checks viewAny, so create/update/delete are never consulted (app/Policies/ProductPolicy.php, routes/web.php:13). A single Gate would be simpler.
formattedPrice() is a plain method rather than an Attribute accessor (app/Models/Product.php:40). Minor.
The sort filter is hand-rolled markup instead of reusing the x-form.select component, and @selected compares against $filters['category'] ?? null (resources/views/products/index.blade.php:10-24).
The new checkbox component also renders @error itself, duplicating x-form.field (resources/views/components/form/checkbox.blade.php:9).
strengths: Search uses filled(), so "0" is a valid search term (probe passed), and LIKE wildcards are escaped.

Well-composed components: x-form.field wraps label, slot and @error, and input/select/textarea compose on top of it. Uses $attributes->class, @selected/@checked, old() with model fallback, and a hidden input for the checkbox.
Thin controllers using to_route()->with('status'), relatedTo/inCategory/search/active #[Scope] scopes, whereBelongsTo and whereKeyNot. The filters array comes from $request->safe()->only().
restrictOnDelete on category FK, composite indexes for the catalogue queries, Model::shouldBeStrict, and eager loading where it is needed.

Strong Pest tests. Datasets cover access for guests and non-admins on every route and each validation rule. followingRedirects proves errors and old input appear in the rendered form (including the selected category). Covers pagination links with preserved filters, page 2 count, empty filters, invalid query input, and an unchecked checkbox.

v.rationale:
I ranked impl-2 first. Both suites pass (impl-2: 44 tests, impl-1: 45), and the two apps are structurally almost identical: same FormRequests, #[Scope] scopes, enum sort, shared product-form component, inline-CSS layout and to_route flash redirects.

The deciding factor was one probe. In impl-1, /products?q=0 returns every product, because the search scope uses `when($term)` and "0" is falsy. impl-2 uses filled(), so that search works. impl-1 also sends someone who opens an invalid filter URL directly to a welcome page that never shows errors, while impl-2 lands them on /products with the errors listed.

On idioms, impl-1 does better in places: @session, an Attribute accessor, a dedicated <x-form.error> component and reuse of the select component in the filter form. It loses ground elsewhere: it builds a collection in the view, wraps everything in __() (including a no-op trans_choice), adds a custom pagination view, and cascade-deletes products when a category is deleted.

impl-2 also has rough edges: query logic inside the enum, and a four-method policy where only viewAny is ever enforced. Its tests are slightly stronger, since they render the redirected form to check that errors and old input actually appear.

bugs: No functional bugs found. As in impl-1, the slug check-then-insert loop can race under concurrent creates and turn into a 500 on the unique index (app/Observers/PostObserver.php:28).
antipatterns: routes/api.php:7-11 – separate PUT and PATCH route lines; `Route::apiResource('posts', ...)->except('show')->scoped(['post' => 'slug'])` would be more idiomatic

v.rationale: The two implementations are nearly identical in structure. Both use an enum, an observer for the slug and published_at, route-level `->can()` with a policy, Form Requests, an API Resource, and modern attribute-based models. The ranking comes down to edge cases I confirmed with throwaway probe tests. impl-1 returns a 500 when a guest calls the API without an Accept: application/json header, because it redirects to a `login` route that doesn't exist. impl-1 also rejects empty query filters with 422 and has no PATCH route. impl-2 handles all three: it returns a JSON 401 for API guests, treats empty filters as absent using `nullable`, and routes PATCH. It also uses race-safe `createOrFirst` for tags and binds posts by slug. impl-1 is slightly more idiomatic in a couple of places: it uses `$request->enum` and `$request->integer`, and it avoids the needless `Http::preventStrayRequests`. Those are minor compared with impl-2's correctness advantages, so impl-2 ranks first.

v.rationale: Both implementations are structurally almost identical: an observer for the slug and published_at, a policy enforced through route-level ->can(), Form Requests, an API Resource that plucks tag names, #[Scope] scopes and attribute-based models. Both suites pass (impl-2 26/26, impl-1 22/22). The probes are what separate them. impl-1 returns a 500 to a guest calling GET /api/posts without an Accept: application/json header, because auth tries to redirect to a login route that doesn't exist. It also has no PATCH route (405), and it rejects empty query filters with a 422. impl-2 handles all three correctly: 401, PATCH works, and empty filters are ignored. impl-2 also uses createOrFirst, which is safe when two requests create the same tag at once, puts a user_id default in the factory, skips the redundant setStatusCode(201), filters from validated() data, and has broader edge-case tests. impl-2's weaknesses are small (put and patch declared as separate route lines, a little test noise), so it ranks first.

bugs: Marking a task done without setting completed_at (e.g. $task->update(['status' => 'done'])) leaves completed_at null, so the task is never counted in tasks_completed_last_7_days. Nothing ties status to completed_at (app/Models/Task.php:17, probe confirmed)

The dashboard uses Cache::remember with no stampede protection. Concurrent misses after an invalidation all recompute the expensive query, and Cache::flexible was not used even though the task allows up to 5 minutes of stale data (app/Services/TeamDashboard.php:16)
antipatterns: app/Services/TeamDashboard.php:16 — Cache::remember plus a hand-rolled version key, where Cache::flexible([secs, 300]) would cover the 'stale OK if recompute is slow' requirement
app/Services/TeamDashboard.php:34 — the version key is itself stored with Cache::remember, so every dashboard read costs two cache round trips
app/Observers/TaskObserver.php:24 — a DB query on every task save just to find the team_id
app/Services/ExchangeRates.php:28-40 — manual block/try/finally release, where the block($secs, $callback) form is shorter
strengths: Routes go through routes/api.php with Sanctum, and guests get a 401 for both JSON and plain requests
Rotating a version key prevents the race where a reader computing old data re-caches it after a forget; the reason is stated in one tight docblock

UserObserver only invalidates when team_id changes or the user is created, so unrelated user saves don't flush the cache
Exchange rates: double-checked fresh cache under the lock, separate fresh and last-known keys, a failure cooldown, timeout(3), and lock timeout falls back to stale or 503
Strong Pest tests: an invalidation dataset covering 10 kinds of change, query-count assertions, failure datasets, and Sleep::fake lock-contention tests
FormRequest normalises case and exposes a typed currency() accessor; #[Scope] attributes and enum casts

bugs: A guest making a non-JSON request to /api/dashboard or /api/exchange-rates/{c} gets a 500 (RouteNotFoundException: Route [login] not defined), because the API routes live in web.php behind the session 'auth' middleware (routes/web.php:11, probe confirmed)

Cache::forget invalidation has a race: a reader that started computing before a write commits can re-cache the old data for up to 5 minutes, which breaks the 'reflected within seconds' requirement under concurrency (app/Support/TeamDashboard.php:40-44)

The dashboard uses Cache::remember with no stampede protection and does not use Cache::flexible despite the stale-tolerant requirement (app/Support/TeamDashboard.php:20)

app/Observers/TaskObserver.php:13-16 — two separate queries on every task save, even when project_id did not change
tests/Feature/ExchangeRatesTest.php:4 — `use Closure;` in a non-namespaced file produces a PHP warning in the test run
tests/Feature/ExchangeRatesTest.php:175 — the 'three second timeout' test only asserts a config value and never checks the timeout actually applied
tests/Feature/ExchangeRatesTest.php:110 — the test says waiting requests reuse the lock holder's result, but it only checks a plain cache hit
tests/Feature/ExchangeRatesTest.php:16-20 — a mutable $this->upstream closure works around Http::fake, which is more indirect than Http::sequence
strengths: The Task saving hook keeps completed_at consistent with status (stamped when done, cleared when reopened)
Uses Cache::lock()->block($wait, $callback), which releases the lock automatically
DB::afterCommit defers invalidation until the transaction commits
Failed fetches are reported with report($e); timeout and lock wait are in config/services.php
Thin invokable controllers, a FormRequest with a typed accessor, and #[Scope] and #[ObservedBy] attributes
Tests cover timeouts via ConnectionException, malformed and empty bodies, cooldown recovery, and the 7-day window moving with travel()

v.rationale: Both suites pass (impl-1: 42 tests, impl-2: 41 tests). The two implementations are close in structure, so the ranking comes down to how robust the caching is and to the bugs the probes found. impl-1 ranks first. It puts the routes in api.php with Sanctum, so guests get a 401 for both JSON and plain requests. Its version-key rotation stops a reader from re-caching data computed before a write committed. Its observers fire after commit and skip unrelated user saves. Its tests are stronger, including lock-contention tests using Sleep::fake. Its main gap is that a task marked done without a completed_at is not counted as completed. impl-2 puts the API routes in web.php behind session auth, so a non-JSON request from a guest returns a 500 (probe confirmed). Its plain Cache::forget leaves the stale-recache race open. It also clears the dashboard cache on any user save (probe confirmed). Its tests are weaker: the 3-second timeout test only checks a config value, one test name overstates what it checks, and a `use Closure;` line causes a warning. On the plus side, impl-2 auto-stamps completed_at and uses the callback form of lock block(). Neither implementation uses Cache::flexible or protects the dashboard against a stampede.

bugs: Minor: Task has no hook that keeps completed_at in step with status. completed_at is fillable and set by hand, so a task marked done without completed_at never counts toward tasks_completed_last_7_days.
Minor: the 'last known' rates expire after 30 days (app/Services/ExchangeRates.php:63). After a month without a successful fetch, the endpoint returns 503 even though rates were once known.
antipatterns: app/Services/TeamDashboard.php:16 uses Cache::remember with a 5-minute TTL. The brief ('stale up to 5 minutes acceptable if recomputing is slow') points at Cache::flexible for stale-while-revalidate, which isn't used.

app/Services/TeamDashboard.php:27-35: invalidation rotates a version key, which means two cache reads per request and an extra UUID entry. It is sound against the read-during-write race, but it is more machinery than forget plus afterCommit.
app/Services/ExchangeRates.php:71-72 hardcodes timeout(3) and connectTimeout(2) while the URL comes from config. This is inconsistent, though acceptable.
app/Http/Controllers/DashboardController.php:15 returns 404 for a user without a team. 403 or an empty dashboard would be clearer.
strengths: Uses the proper API layer: routes/api.php via withRouting(api:), Sanctum auth, and redirectGuestsTo plus shouldRenderJsonWhen. Plain non-JSON guest requests get 401 and validation failures get 422, both verified by probe.

Observers implement ShouldHandleEventsAfterCommit and forget each team separately. Moving a task, project or user to an uncached team correctly invalidates the old team (probed). A transaction followed by several updates also invalidates correctly (probed).
UserObserver only invalidates on team_id changes or creation, which avoids pointless cache busts on profile edits.

The exchange-rate flow is solid: Cache::lock()->block(5) with release in finally, a re-check of the fresh cache under the lock, a failure cooldown so a down API isn't hammered, and stale or 503 fallback. Http timeout(3) is set.

The lock tests are excellent: Sleep::fake and whenFakingSleep simulate a concurrent lock holder, either filling the cache or failing, and assert the API is never called. Http::sequence covers several failure modes.
The 'reflects changes immediately' dataset covers 10 mutation types compactly, plus tests for project and user moves and a query-count check for cache hits.

bugs: app/Support/TeamDashboard.php:44: `$keys->each(Cache::forget(...))`. Collection::each stops when the callback returns false, and Cache::forget returns false for a missing key on the array, redis and file stores. Keys are ordered new-team first, so when a task, project or user moves to a team with no cached dashboard, the OLD team's dashboard is never cleared and stays stale for up to 5 minutes. Probes confirmed this: a task moved to another team still showed open_task_count 1, and a member who switched teams still showed member_count 2. A task-to-other-project move also breaks this way.

The API routes live in routes/web.php under a prefix with session 'auth' middleware (routes/web.php:11). A plain (non-JSON) guest GET /api/dashboard returns 500 because there is no login route (probed). Invalid-currency requests without JSON headers would also go through web-style redirect handling.
1 PHPUnit warning in the suite: tests/Feature/ExchangeRatesTest.php:4 has `use Closure;` in the global namespace, which has no effect.
antipatterns: app/Support/TeamDashboard.php:20 uses Cache::remember with a 5-minute TTL instead of Cache::flexible, despite the brief describing stale-while-revalidate.
routes/web.php:11 puts JSON API endpoints in the web route file with session auth instead of routes/api.php plus Sanctum or a token guard.
tests/Feature/ExchangeRatesTest.php:16-20 adds a mutable $this->upstream indirection around Http::fake to work around stub ordering. Http::sequence or re-faking would be simpler.
tests/Feature/ExchangeRatesTest.php:175-182: the 'three second timeout' test only asserts a config value and the host. It doesn't verify that the timeout is applied.

The tests for 'another request is refreshing' (tests/Feature/ExchangeRatesTest.php:86-108) rely on lock_wait=0, so the waiting path where a waiter reuses the holder's result is never really exercised.
strengths: Clean Task model: #[Scope] attributes, enum cast, and a saving hook that keeps completed_at consistent with status.
Invalidation is deferred with DB::afterCommit, with keys computed eagerly. It handles old and new team ids using getOriginal in saved.

FetchExchangeRates is well structured: a lock with block(), the callback form auto-releases, a double-check under the lock, a forever 'last-known' key, a failure cooldown, report() on HTTP failures, and timeout plus URL in config/services.php.
Good test breadth for invalidation scenarios and failure datasets (timeout, 5xx, malformed, empty rates), with travel() used for TTL checks.

v.rationale:
I rank impl-1 first. Both suites pass (impl-2: 41 tests, impl-1: 42), and the two share very similar structures: invokable controllers, a FormRequest that uppercases the route parameter, #[Scope] scopes, the same HasManyThrough dashboard query, and lock, double-check, cooldown and stale fallback for exchange rates. v.rationale:
I ranked impl-2 first and impl-1 second. Both test suites pass: 15 tests for impl-1, 18 for impl-2.

**Shared behaviour:** Both use the same core design: a form request, a policy that returns denyAsNotFound(), a 10-minute temporarySignedRoute to a signed download route outside auth, and Storage::download for the attachment. They checked the same in every probe:
- Text disguised as a PDF gets 422.
- An SVG disguised as a PNG gets 422.
- A real PDF named .html is stored under a random .pdf name.
- A tampered expires value gets 403.
- Unicode and '%' in the filename produce a correct Content-Disposition.

Neither has a real functional bug.

**Why impl-2 ranks higher:** The difference is in idioms and how robust the confidential storage is:
- It pins the private disk explicitly. impl-1 relies on the default disk, which an env value can change.
- It uses the fluent File::types()->max() rule.
- It declares authorization on the route with ->can().
- It caps original_name at the column length.
- Its download test calls forgetGuards(), so it really proves the link works without logging in, and it checks the file contents. impl-1's equivalent test still has a logged-in Sanctum user.

**Where impl-2 loses points:**
- Three controllers instead of one.
- A factory without a user_id default.
- An unneeded Http::preventStrayRequests() in the tests.

**impl-1:** It's slightly simpler. It's a solid second.

- Add `customer_id` as a nullable column with no constraint.
- Build the composite indexes `(customer_id, created_at)` and `(customer_id, status, created_at)`, which fit the endpoint's query.
- Add the foreign key with `nullOnDelete` while foreign key checks are off, so MySQL can add it in place without copying the table.

- sparse ids with a large gap
- the SQL actually generated
- `updated_at` staying put on both matched and unmatched rows
- an empty status filter

- It uses framework features where impl-1 hand-rolls them. It passes a Builder straight to `update()`, where impl-1 uses `DB::raw` with `toSql()`, which would break if the subquery ever had bindings. It calls `Schema::withoutForeignKeyConstraints()`, where impl-1 writes its own helper.
- It adds an `id` tie-breaker to the sort, so pagination is stable.
- It validates `status` with a FormRequest.
- Its tests cover much more: multiple chunks, output counts, index existence, pagination, 404s and validation.

**Where impl-1 is better.** It implements `Isolatable`, so two backfills can't overlap, and it avoids impl-2's costly min/max scan over the NULL `customer_id` entries.

Both implementations find the same four root causes and fix them in much the same way. Both test suites pass: impl-1 has 14 tests, impl-2 has 12. The four causes are:
1. A catch block swallowed exceptions.
2. The dispatcher re-queued every unsynced row each minute.
3. withoutOverlapping() on the scheduled task defaulted to a 24-hour mutex.
4. chunk() paginated by offset over the column it was mutating.

My probes separated them:
- **Backed-up queue:** impl-1 uses ShouldBeUnique with UniqueFor set to the same 1800s CLAIM_SECONDS constant as its claim. This blocked duplicate enqueues: two direct dispatches gave 1 queued job, and a 20-minute backlog still had 1. impl-2 relies on WithoutOverlapping->dontRelease(), which only blocks concurrent runs. It gave 2 queued jobs in both cases, so the backlog problem is only partly fixed, though its fresh() check limits duplicate POSTs.
- **Existing behaviour:** impl-1 keeps it, logging and recording crm_last_error on every attempt. impl-2 drops the logging and only records the error after the final failure.
- **Where impl-2 is stronger:** a cleaner job with a failed() hook, timeout and deleteWhenMissingModels, plus a slightly tighter claim query.
- **Where impl-1 is weaker:** it repeats the claim predicate and has one test whose time travel does nothing.

On balance impl-1 is more correct and uses current Laravel 13 queue attributes, so it ranks first.

I rank impl-2 first and impl-1 second; it's close.

Both fixed the same four root causes:
1. The job's try/catch swallowed the exception, so failed syncs never retried and never reached failed_jobs.
2. Every scheduler run re-dispatched every unsynced subscriber without checking whether one was already queued, so the CRM got the same subscriber many times.
3. The scheduled task's withoutOverlapping() lock lasts 24 hours by default, which is why `crm:dispatch-sync` stopped for about a day after the container was killed.
4. The normalise command used chunk() while updating the column it filters on, which skips about half the rows; both switched to chunkById().

Both add backoff, an atomic claim on crm_sync_queued_at with a stale timeout, and a fresh() check in the job so a subscriber that is already synced isn't posted again. Both suites pass (impl-2: 12 tests; impl-1: 14 tests).

I probed each with a real database queue:
- 5 scheduler runs while the queue is backed up: both left one job per subscriber.
- An outage that used up all retries, then a later run: both re-dispatched and synced the subscriber.
- One failure, then success on retry: both synced it with nothing in failed_jobs.
- A subscriber deleted while its job is queued: impl-1 put the job in failed_jobs; impl-2 discarded it cleanly.

Why impl-2 wins:
- **Simpler error handling.** It removes the try/catch and uses a failed() hook. impl-1 keeps a log-update-rethrow block that writes the error on every attempt.
- **Covers a second stuck-lock case.** It gives the per-subscriber job lock an expiry, so a killed worker can't hold it forever. impl-1 removed that lock entirely.
- **Handles deleted subscribers.**
- **Tighter claim.** Its claim also checks crm_synced_at; impl-1's doesn't.

Where impl-1 is stronger:
- It uses the newer Laravel 13 queue attributes and the framework's built-in unique-job support (ShouldBeUnique).
- Its main query skips rows that are already claimed, while impl-2 runs one wasted update per in-flight row every minute.
- It has slightly broader tests, though one of them proves less than its name says.

Those idiom wins don't outweigh impl-1's deleted-subscriber bug, its repeated rethrow block and its duplicated query condition.

Both cover the core queue requirements: createOrFirst for idempotent storage, a per-event WithoutOverlapping lock, a shared 10/s RateLimited limiter, backoff with retryUntil, and failed() recording the error. impl-1 wins on the idioms that carry most weight here. It uses MassPrunable with model:prune, its order transitions are guarded so out-of-order events are safe, its queue attributes are the most modern, and its tests are much stronger because they run a real database queue for 5xx backoff, giving up after the retry limit, rate-limit release and the overlap lock. Its bugs are that the admin API uses session auth on the stateless api group, the validated() payload drops fields, and the receipt notification isn't queued. impl-2 does better on transactional safety (a transaction with lockForUpdate, ShouldQueueAfterCommit) and uses proper Sanctum auth. However, a probe found a real data bug: a late payment.succeeded moves a refunded order back to paid and emails the customer a receipt. It also drops envelope fields, hand-rolls the pruning instead of using Prunable, adds an extra redispatch command, and has weaker tests where retries are only simulated. I judged impl-2's wrong-state email the more damaging bug, which together with impl-1's better tests and pruning idiom puts impl-1 narrowly ahead.

v.rationale:
Both suites pass (impl-1: 38 tests, impl-2: 37). Each has sound core queue mechanics: createOrFirst on a unique event_id, WithoutOverlapping per event, a shared RateLimited limiter, Backoff and retryUntil, 4xx sent to fail(), a 429 Retry-After release, and failed() recording the error.

impl-2 ranks first, narrowly, because more of its parts work as they would in production:
- The order update, refund and event status change run in one transaction with a row lock.
- The receipt is queued and sent only after commit (ShouldQueueAfterCommit), and the webhook dispatch uses afterCommit.
- A missing order fails at once instead of retrying.
- The admin endpoint can actually be reached with a Sanctum token.

Its probed bugs:
- A 302 redirect instead of 422 for an invalid payload sent without an Accept header.
- Unknown event types are rejected and never stored.
- A refunded order can flip back to Paid when a late payment.succeeded arrives.
- It hand-rolls a prune command where MassPrunable would do, and adds an unrequested redispatch command.

impl-1 has the better pruning (MassPrunable with model:prune), stores unknown types, has safer order state transitions, and has outstanding real-queue tests. Its problems weigh more, though:
- The admin endpoint uses the session `auth` guard on the stateless API, so admins can't really authenticate. A guest request without an Accept header returns 500 ('Route [login] not defined').
- The receipt notification is synchronous.
- There is no transaction around the order, refund and event updates.
- A missing order is retried for about 40 minutes.
- The README says failed events can be replayed with queue:retry, but the job skips failed events, so the replay does nothing.
